What I am reasonably confident of (from memory):
(1) The Manheim Used Vehicle Value Index peaked at about 236 in January 2022. It fell through 2023, then traded in a relatively tight band of about 199-209 through 2024-2025, still well above the pre-pandemic level of about 140 in 2019. In April 2025 it briefly jumped to about 208 after the new US auto tariffs (25% Section 232 tariffs on imported vehicles and parts, effective spring 2025) pulled demand forward. For the rest of 2025 it ran low-single-digit % above year-earlier levels. I could not verify any 2026 monthly print.
(2) Structural support for older cheap cars through 2026-2027: low new-car production in 2020-2023 and very low lease originations mean few 1-5-year-old used cars. Buyers were pushed into older, cheaper vehicles, and listings under $15k became scarce (the average used listing is about $25k; the sub-$15k share is well below pre-pandemic). High auto-loan rates add to the same shift. Tariffs raised new-car prices and parts/repair costs, which also supports used values.
(3) Headwinds for 2027: lease returns start to recover as 2023-2025 leases mature, adding late-model supply. That mainly softens 1-4-year-old values; the effect on 12-15-year-old $8-13k cars is indirect and smaller. Other risks: a recession or rising unemployment, subprime loan stress, and tariff reversal.
(4) Cox Automotive's public forecasts have generally called for broadly stable wholesale values (low-single-digit year-over-year changes) rather than a crash. I could not confirm the exact 2026 or 2027 forecast figures.

Base case used in the model estimates: the market level is flat, 0% +/- 5%, from Oct 2026 to Aug 2027. On top of that, age and mileage depreciation per model:
- Toyota/Lexus 12-15 years old: about 5.5-7% a year private party (about 0.8-1.1% a month including 9k miles).
- GX 470: about 3% a year (about 0.5% a month).
- IS 250 and Prius: about 7-8% a year (about 1.1-1.3% a month).
- Land Rover: about 15-17% a year (about 2.2-2.5% a month).
- Trade and instant-offer values fall faster, by about 2 points a year more.
- Mileage adjustment: $0.04-0.08 per mile. For 9,000 miles that is $360-720.
A -5% or +5% market scenario moves the Aug-2027 private value by about $400-600 on a $9-10k car.
seasonality_notes:
UNVERIFIED (no live search available this session). These are general patterns from model knowledge.

(1) National wholesale (Manheim, not seasonally adjusted) usually rises January to March or April as tax refunds arrive (IRS refunds peak in February-March). It then drifts down May-December, with the softest stretch in October-December. Retail asking prices for cheap cars follow the same pattern with a lag. Tax season (February-April) is the strongest time to sell. November-December (holidays, winter, dealers clearing year-end inventory) is generally the best time to buy. iSeeCars-type deal studies have pointed to late-year months for the most discounted used listings (my recollection).

(2) This plan buys in October 2026, which is seasonally soft and favorable. It sells in August 2027, after the spring peak but typically still at or slightly above the prior October's level. The seasonal effect of the round trip is about neutral to +2%. I applied +1% for most Toyota/Lexus models, +2% for student-favored models (Corolla, Camry, Prius, ES, RAV4), 0% for Land Rover, and 0% on dealer offers.

(3) Wisconsin factor: AWD and 4WD SUVs (RAV4, RX, Highlander, GX) see their strongest local demand around the first snow (October-December). Selling an AWD SUV in August forgoes that bump. Buying one in October, by contrast, happens at a seasonally firm time for AWD.

(4) Madison August effect (plausible, but I found no hard data this session): Madison's lease year traditionally turns over in mid-August (around August 14-15), and UW-Madison fall classes start right after Labor Day. International and new graduate students arrive in mid-to-late August and look for cheap, reliable cars, often through 小红书, WeChat groups and Facebook Marketplace. That is a genuine buyer pool for a well-documented Toyota or Lexus. But departing graduates also sell in May and in July-August, so supply rises too. The net premium is modest; I assumed +1-2%, unverified.

Practical timing: list about 3-5 weeks before leaving (mid-July). Offer a handover date that matches new students' arrival. Get CarMax, Carvana and KBB Instant Cash Offer quotes in July as a guaranteed floor. Leave a buffer to complete the title transfer before leaving the country.
dealer_vs_private_gap_notes:
UNVERIFIED (from model knowledge; no live data this session). For 10-15-year-old cars priced around $8-13k:
- Dealer retail asking is typically about 12-25% above private-party value.
- Trade-in and instant cash offers (KBB ICO, CarMax, Carvana) are typically about 20-35% below private-party value.
- So the full dealer spread from retail to wholesale is about $3,500-5,500 on a $10-12k Toyota or Lexus, and about $5,000-7,500 on a Land Rover.

Why the spread is so large on cheap cars: dealers need reconditioning ($500-1,500), auction and transport fees, floor-plan costs, and a fixed-dollar profit. That profit is a big percentage of a cheap car's price. Dealers also usually wholesale cars over about 10 years old or 150k miles at auction rather than retail them, so they bid at the auction price minus fees.

How the buyers compare:
- CarMax: appraisals are good for 7 days. Offers on older, high-mileage cars are auction-based and often at or below the low end of KBB trade-in.
- Carvana: also buys old cars, but offers drop steeply with age and miles.
- KBB Instant Cash Offer: a redeemable offer from participating dealers, usually in the KBB trade-in "fair to good" range.
- Peddle: aimed at high-mileage or damaged cars and usually the lowest.
- For older Land Rovers the dealer discount is extra-large because of repair-liability risk.

Implications for this buyer, under my estimates:
- The single biggest cost lever is the channel, not the model. Buying at dealer retail and selling to a dealer loses about $4,700-5,600 on a Toyota or Lexus (about $6,300-7,500 on a Land Rover). That is 5-6 times the pure 10.5-month depreciation.
- Buying and selling privately loses only about $600-1,100 on a Toyota or Lexus, and about $1,900-2,000 on a Land Rover.
- Buying at dealer retail but selling privately loses about $2,100-2,700.
- So the "捡漏" strategy is to buy from a private seller (or a dealer car priced at or below private-party value) and sell privately to incoming students. Use dealer instant offers only as a backstop.
- Note that Wisconsin collects sales tax on private-party purchases at DMV registration too (5% state plus 0.5% Dane County). Buying privately avoids the dealer's fee but not the tax.

Key findings (estimates):
(1) Expected private-party loss from about October 2026 to August 2027 with 9,000 miles, if bought and sold privately:
- GX 470: about $600 (-5%)
- Corolla, Camry, ES 350, RAV4, RX 350: about $800-900 (-8 to -10%)
- Highlander, Prius: about $1,000 (-11%)
- IS 250 AWD: about $1,100 (-12.5%)
- Land Rover LR4, RR Sport, Evoque: about $1,900-2,000 (-21 to -23%), plus large repair tail risk (5.0 V8 timing chain, air suspension, 9-speed transmission).

(2) Expected August 2027 dealer or instant offers:
- Toyota/Lexus: about $5,000-6,800 (GX about $8,100)
- Land Rover: about $3,300-4,200

(3) The channel matters far more than the model. The dealer retail-to-trade spread is about $4,700-5,600 for Toyota/Lexus and $6,300-7,500 for Land Rover. So the lowest-cost plan is to buy privately or at a below-market dealer price, then sell privately in Madison in mid-July to mid-August to incoming students (小红书, WeChat groups, Facebook Marketplace), with CarMax, Carvana or KBB ICO quotes as a floor.

(4) Best value retention in the $8-13k band:
- GX 470 (a rust-free example; but about 15 mpg and 170k+ miles)
- RAV4 AWD, Corolla, Camry, ES 350: these combine low depreciation with the easiest resale to students.

Land Rover models are poor fits for a 10-month hold. Toyota and Lexus lead value-retention and longevity rankings (iSeeCars, Consumer Reports, J.D. Power), while Land Rover sits near the bottom. This is from recollection and was not re-verified here.

(5) Market backdrop: wholesale values were stable in about the 200-209 Manheim band through 2024-2025, supported by a shortage of late-model used cars and 2025 tariffs. The base case is flat, +/-5%, through August 2027. Seasonality from an October buy to an August sell is about neutral to +2%. AWD SUVs would fetch more if sold in October-December rather than August.
